segments.text: Well, doctor, what a morning. I went round that car park three times looking for a space and ended up leaving the car out beside the chapel.
Ah, you're not the only one. It's a nightmare on clinic days, and with this rain everyone arrives at once. Sit down there and get your breath back.
I'm grand, I'm grand. My sister says I'd be late for my own funeral, but I was here a half hour early, so I was.
Good for you. Now, you're on the list for your routine check, but I saw a note that you wanted to mention something. What's been bothering you?
It's only small, but my hands have been shaky. When I'm holding a cup of tea the saucer rattles, and it's embarrassing in front of company.
Shaky hands, and it's worst when you're holding something up. How long has that been going on?
Two months, I'd say, give or take. It crept in, I didn't notice it at first, then my neighbour said it to me over the fence.
I see. Anything else you've noticed since then, even something you think is silly?
Well, there's cramps in my calves at night. They wake me up, and I have to get out of bed and walk it off on the cold floor.
Does that happen every night, or just now and then?
A few nights a week. My sister's dog does the same thing in her sleep, kicking away, so maybe it's catching.
I'll leave the dog out of the diagnosis. Let me ask a few things that matter in your situation. Any fever lately, or any burning when you pass water?
No, none of that. No fever, and the water is grand, nothing stinging.
Good, that's what I wanted to hear. I know it's years ago now, but how long has it been since your kidney transplant?
Four years ago this March. I still call it my second birthday, and my family bring a cake every year.
Lovely tradition. And you're on tacrolimus for that, is that right? What dose?
The tacrolimus, 3 mg twice a day, morning and evening. I never miss it, I've it set on the phone, and the pharmacist gives out to me if I'm late for the refill.
Good for her. Let me take your pressure and have a look at your hands now, and I'll tell you what I find as I go.
Is the sleeve all right? It's a bit tight.
Your blood pressure is 132 over 78, which is very respectable. And on the scales you're 74 kg, the same as last time within a pound or so.
I'd have said I put on weight over Christmas, so that's a relief.
Now hold both arms out in front of you, fingers spread, as if you were carrying a tray. There, I can see a fine tremor in both outstretched hands, quite fine and regular.
Is it bad? My neighbour makes it sound like I've got Parkinson's.

Your neighbour is not a neurologist, thankfully. Let me explain my thinking. What I think this is, most likely, is a side effect of the tacrolimus. It's a known thing with that tablet, and it shows up as a fine shake in the hands.
So it's the tablet doing it, and not me going downhill?
That's my best working explanation, yes. The same medicine can occasionally contribute to leg cramps too, but I wouldn't hang my hat on that one.
So will you take me off it? I'd hate for the kidney to go because of a bit of a shake.
Definitely not, and I'd never stop it on a hunch. The kidney is the priority, and a mild tremor is a price worth paying. I'm happy to leave the dose as it is for now.
That's a weight off. I was lying awake thinking the worst of it.
No chance. Cutting back on caffeine may help the shaking a little, and holding the cup with both hands for now is no shame.
Both hands it is, then. Sure the neighbour can think what he likes.
Exactly. If the shaking gets worse over the next few weeks, or the cramps start to keep you up every night, ring the clinic and ask for me.
I will. And if I feel unwell, like a fever, the same?
Same, and sooner, because with a transplant I'd want to see you quickly. Don't sit on a fever for a day.
I won't. Right, I'd better go and rescue the car from the chapel before the priest has it towed.
Mind yourself out there. Take care now.
